thread.title: Here's Why Stocks Could Be Headed A Lot Lower From Here - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)

author: Victor Dergunov
title: Here's Why Stocks Could Be Headed A Lot Lower From Here - SPDR S&P 500 Trust ETF (NYSEARCA:SPY)
text:
Source: MetalsNews.com
Here’s Why Stocks Could Be Headed Lower From Here The economic atmosphere surrounding the S&P 500/SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) has turned decisively more bearish in recent weeks. In addition to various concerns, many valuations are still extremely elevated, Fed policy is starting to significantly impact growth, rates are inverting, and continued economic weakness could potentially lead to an earnings recession. Moreover, there are now significant political risks hanging over the market, and the technical image is beginning to breakdown.
Due to the weakening economic image, lackluster sentiment is likely to persist, and could potentially worsen. Furthermore, absent a concrete catalyst to take stocks substantially higher, momentum will likely continue to press the S&P 500 to the downside going forward.
About SPY
SPY is the first major and most popular ETF in the world. It's designed to mimic the exact movement of the S&P 500. The SPY index fund has roughly $253.5 billion in net assets, and each share in the fund represents a fraction of the holdings.
SPY provides investors with exposure to the S&P 500 index, which is widely regarded as the most significant stock market average for U.S. equities. Since SPY tracks the exact movements of the S&P 500, I will use SPY and the S&P 500 interchangeably throughout this article.
Technicals Breaking Down I want to first draw attention to the apparent breakdown in the techncials surrounding the S&P 500.
SPX 1-Year
Source: StockCharts.com
The S&P 500 just registered its first series of closes below the crucial 2,600 level since early April (the height of the early 2018 correction). Any further decisive price action below this level will be perceived as extremely negative from a technical standpoint and is likely to weigh on the overall psychological image surrounding the stock market.
In addition, we see that the 50-day MA just crossed bellow the 200-day MA, another very bearish development and the S&P 500 is starting to make lower lows and lower highs. Moreover, declines are very orderly, and there is no real sense of panic in the air. The recent price action is no longer indicative of a correction, but is much more in tune to the type of price action one would expect to see in the early stages of a bear market.
Other Red Flags While the S&P 500 is down by about 13.5%, the Nasdaq 100 ( QQQ ) is down by about 17%, the Russell 2000 ( IWM ) is now off by 21%, and the FAANNG+M+BAT names are down (on average) by roughly 36% (peak to trough 52-week period) .
SPY data by YCharts
This illustrates that the higher alpha names, the leaders of the latest bull run are now the clear laggards, or leaders to the downside. Moreover, this phenomenon is likely to persist, and could cause other sectors to follow the former leaders into bear market territory.
In fact, another clear red flag is the exodus into “safer perceived” equities. If we look at recent sector performance we can clearly see unusual rotation into defensive sectors like consumer staples, real estate, and most notably utilities.
The reason I say that this rotation is unusual is because it is drastically different from what we witnessed in the prior correction of early 2018. In the “first correction”, just about everything tanked, FANGs, industrials, healthcare, and yes, consumer staples and utilities.
This price action was indicative of a short-term phenomenon, when investors temporarily panic and sell just about everything in sight, regardless of sector for the most part. However, what we are seeing now is far more deliberate.
We’re seeing significant capital rotate away from riskier, economically sensitive sectors, consumer discretionary, energy, financials, materials, industrials, technology, even communication services, and into essentially the three most defensive sectors, consumer staples, real estate, and utilities.
This type of price action is much more indicative of something you would expect to see in the early stages of a bear market as investors begin to move away from the highly sensitive sectors, and into much more defensive segments of the economy.
This is why utilities are at around an all-time high right now, while real estate is close to its 52-week high, and consumer staples are only off by around 5% from recent highs. On the other hand, sectors like energy are off by 21%, financials are down by 20%, materials are down by 20%, technology is off by 15.5%, consumer discretionary are down by 16%, industrials are off by 17%, etc.
XLU data by YCharts
Despite the S&P 500 being off by “only” 13.5%, most segments of the economy are either in bear market territory already, or are very close to dipping into bear markets. The good news is that this is likely still relatively early in the process, and market participants still have time to either rotate into safer segments, implement hedging strategies, reduce overall exposure to stocks and so on.
Furthermore, while the more defensive sectors are likely to outperform, their declines may also be considerable when the true bear market materializes. We may still be just on the cusp of any real declines, and stocks in aggregate could potentially fall a lot further over the next months and years.
So, why are stocks likely to fall further, and what would be an appropriate level to see the stock market bottom?
Many Valuations Still Sky-High When I write about valuations being high people sometimes disagree with me. The counterargument to high valuations is that many companies are trading at relatively cheap valuations. However, this is all relative. For instance, if you are talking about a company like Micron ( MU ) which trades at a 4 times forward earnings multiple , forward multiples and projections can be deceiving due to the nature of the company’s business.
Even Apple ( AAPL ), which trades at an 11.35 forward earning multiple may not be cheap if iPhone sales begin to stumble in future quarters. The point is that a company’s forward multiple is only as good as its current earnings projections.
The thing about projections in an economic slowdown is that they often get slashed, companies miss earnings, they end up reporting much lower EPS than were expected, and it turns out the stocks were never that cheap to begin with.
Another factor to consider is that when valuations are discussed I prefer to focus on stock valuations in general, meaning the average valuation of an S&P 500 company relative to the historic valuation of an average S&P 500 company.
Even more I like to look at the CAPE, cyclically adjusted P/E , also known as the Schiller P/E. This ratio looks at real EPS over a 10-year period, providing a “smoother” gauge than the typical P/E. So, for context, let’s see where the S&P 500’s valuation is today per the these key ratios.
The S&P 500’s P/E ratio is currently at about 19.94 , which is well below its recent high of roughly 24, but is still much higher than its historical median 14.73. Perhaps even more telling, the Schiller P/E ratio is currently at 28.20, just starting to come off its second highest level ever of about 33.5, and still far higher than the median 15.69.
Schiller P/E Historic
Source: Multpl.com
So, let’s break this down. For the S&P 500, just to get back to its historic median, the Schiller P/E would need to decline by about 46%. For the S&P 500’s overall P/E ratio to get back to its median range it would have to decline by an additional 26%.
We are essentially talking about the S&P 500 having to decline by another 26 – 46% from current levels so that these valuation metrics could return to their historical averages. Another factor to consider is that in a bear market valuations don’t typically decline to their historic average, they overshoot to the downside, and sometimes by a lot.
Therefore, stocks could potentially fall a lot further if this is indeed the start of a bear market. A decline of 26% would bring the S&P 500 down to about the 1,925 level, a 46% decline would compress the average all the way down to the 1,400 level, and anything below that would be paramount to the ultra-violent declines witnessed at the height of the financial crisis in 2008/2009.
So, why would P/E ratios fall back to their historic averages?
Well, for one, bull markets can’t last forever, things almost always revert to their mean, there is always a “boom bust cycle”, and the Fed appears to be leading the economy into its next recession.
Fed Policy Impacting Growth Expansions don’t last forever, and there is no such thing as perfect monetary policy. At the end of the day the world is not perfect, and recessions are a normal phenomenon in an economic cycle. A recession is essentially an equalizing force that balances things out after all the malinvestment, and excess credit has been created and accumulated during a boom period.
Record lasting easy monetary policy has led to the possibility for all the excesses to be created in the economy, and tightening monetary policy is bringing about the opposite. Taking away ultra-easy credit is leading to a slowdown in the economy, and could ultimately lead to significant deleveraging, which would likely trigger a substantial recession.
The Fed has now raised interest rates multiple times in the span of several years. The zero-interest rate policy era market participants had become so accustomed to over the last decade is over, and things are starting to look much different already.
Alongside with rising rates, the Fed is also implementing its quantitative tightening program QT, which also causes bond rates to go higher, while essentially sucking liquidity out of the financial system at the same time.
Higher interest rates, and higher bond yields pose several difficulties to stocks, as one, they offer a competing asset class which delivers a “safe” steady yield from owning government, or corporate debt. And two, the cost of browning goes up as rates on credit increase, and credit requirements tighten, putting strain on the economy, and corporate profits at the same time.
There is currently about a 70% chance that the Fed will raise rates on December 19 th , which implies that rates will likely go up to 2.25-2.5% level soon. Yes, this is still relatively low by historical standards, yet an important factor to consider is that the U.S. as a nation, the U.S. consumer, and the U.S. corporate sector have never had so much debt as they do now.
I will save a detailed debt discussion for another article, but the main point here is that interest rates don’t need to go as high as they were 10, or 20 years to have a significantly negative impact on the economy. All interest rates need to do is go high enough to destabilize the status quo, and cause growth to decelerate. We appear to be at this level already, and any further interest rate increases could pose significant threats to the U.S. economy. Furthermore, it is possible that interest rates even at current or slightly higher levels are high enough to tip the economy into a recession relatively soon.
Inflation and GDP Slowing For evidence of slower growth, we can look at inflation, which has come down substantially from recent highs. We’ve seen CPI inflation come off its highs , as well as PCE, and PPI as well. CPI and other inflation levels are at around their lowest levels for the year, and could continue to slump. This is likely partly due to the Fed’s tightening, and could be in part due to the very late stage cycle of this current economic expansion.
We saw a big jump in GDP growth this year, to a 4.2% print in Q2 , and a 3.5% print in Q3. However, this appears to be a short-lived phenomenon as Q4 and next year estimates are substantially lower. The higher GDP burst was propelled by the late cycle tax and fiscal stimuli, the effects of which are likely to be transient and could create a substantial hangover effect going forward. Therefore, next year’s GDP could come in well below current estimates of about 2.7%.
Earnings Misses Could Continue We’ve seen lots of companies miss earnings, and offer disappointing guidance in past quarters. Just think Nvidia , Apple , and many others. Some people may be saying “but many of these companies are reporting record earnings”. Yes, it’s true, but wouldn’t you expect many companies to report record earnings towards the end of an economic cycle during a time of peak earnings?
The main point is that forward guidance is starting to come in weaker than expected in many cases, and this phenomenon may only be starting. Earnings projections were based on continued robust economic growth. Yet, with growth slowing, many companies found their growth projections impossible to keep up with. This trend could continue, and may ultimately lead to an earnings recession, where companies report lower QoQ, and/or YoY earnings for several quarters. Naturally, this would not be a welcomed development in the stock market.
Inverting Interest Rates We’ve seen rates narrow, and some invert even. For instance, the 2-year T-note now provides a higher yield than the 5-year. This indicates that investors are focused on accumulating longer dated treasuries, in an attempt to lock in the highest long-term rate possible now, before the Fed pushes long-term rates lower again.
30 Year Treasury Rate data by YCharts
Why would bond investors believe the Fed was likely to push rates lower? Because an economic recession during which the Fed would likely need to reverse policy is becoming a lot likelier.
Political Risk If all the technical and economic problems weren’t enough, there is now significant political risk hanging over the market as well. Most notably, it is not clear what will come out of the Mueller investigation . Another pressing issue is the looming government shutdown . It is not clear if a deal on the border wall will be reached, and if not a government shutdown could ensue, which may put additional weight on stocks.
Source: VanityFair.com
What’s the Catalyst to Take Stocks Higher? A key factor that appears to be missing from the equation is a concrete catalyst that will bring stocks higher. And not just marginally higher from current levels, but preferably back up to the recent highs, and then on to new all-time highs. There appear to be plenty of catalysts capable of sending stocks lower from here, but positive catalysts appear to be more difficult to come by these days.
2 Possible Wildcards
There are two possible wild cards, the Fed, and a China trade deal. If the Fed were to forgo its interest rate hike on December 19 th , and signal that the tightening path may be close to completion, stocks could react very favorably. Whether this will be enough to reestablish the uptrend and take stocks to new all-time highs is unlikely in my view. However, a short-term rally seems likely in this scenario. Also, the announcement of a beneficial trade deal with China could have a similar effect.
The Bottom Line The technical image surrounding the S&P 500 is deteriorating. In conjunction, various fundamental factors including high valuations, flattening/inverting rates, slower growth, tightening Fed, and other elements are pointing to a challenging time for stocks going forward.
Whether this is another correction or the start of a bear market remains to be seen. However, what is clear is that this has turned into a tumultuous stock market for many market participants. This phenomenon will likely cause many investors to rotate more capital towards bonds, and other alternative investments, as well as safer equities, like consumer staples, real estate, and utilities.
The bottom line is that the declines in stocks may still be in the very early stages, and there could be substantially more down side going forward. Therefore, it may be wise to increase cash positions, rotate to alternative asset classes (i.e. bonds, gold, etc.), rotate to safer, defensive, dividend paying stocks, decrease overall equity exposure, implement hedging and/or option strategy, and so on.
